summary: Hold for a rules problem only: fix (1), the central fix, runs the self-check in a torch.multiprocessing spawn child or subprocess, and TASK.md says a submission that 'starts processes' is rejected (this workspace treats subprocesses as a violation, e.g. the cuobjdump check dropped in muse_attention_decode full-decode-cuda-fp8-qk-mma). Re-mint with fixes (2)-(4) and the per-kernel in-process sync/print diagnostics, no child process, run as `okc check` rather than submit, and the rewrite is otherwise sound to proceed.
justification: The mechanism is plausible and the profile supports it. In FINDINGS (master f1f2f35), Marlin is 271.6/326.1 us at verify_16 sliding/full and 443.2/449.7 us at verify_32. That is 63%/51% and 70%/47% of those shapes, against whole-layer floors of 126.6/188.7/143.8/267.2 us. The MoE weight stream for 32 local NVFP4 experts at T=128/256 is near-dense, so Marlin, which re-streams experts per block_m tile, runs well below 4.8 TB/s. Expert-once swap-AB, with tokens on the N side of m16n8k16 and each expert's weight streamed once per <=64-route chunk, is the right shape of fix on H200 without wgmma. The expected directions fit the weights: verify_16/32 faster, decode_*/verify_1 (T<=32 and T=8) flat because the gate excludes them. The ~150/~200 us targets (about 1.5x the MoE floor) are ambitious but physically reachable. The fix diagnosis follows REWRITE_READ_2026-10-25 section 5. The two never-judge-proven PTX forms (createpolicy.fractional + cp.async L2::cache_hint with a 64-bit policy, and the fma.rn.bf16x2 dequant with a -0 addend) are swapped for forms that dense-chain and splitkv already run on the judge. That is the right first move. The muse_moe_w4a16 sibling died the same way with no route-list kernel, which points at the shared GEMM body. WEAKEST LINK: the faulting opcode was never pinned. If the trap is a .sync.aligned collective (ldmatrix/mma.sync) run by a non-converged warp, from the producer/consumer meta lambdas or the per-thread `rows[i] = p < n ? ...` paths around the item boundaries, neither swap fixes it, and the run dies again. Without the child process, nothing can recover from a sticky 715 in-process, so a second fault costs the whole run (0/0 tests) and gives only the last-printed kernel name as the next clue.
confounders: stack-align-par-sidestream-sliding1: master's T>32 path runs the parallel moe_align plus the expert_map gather on the side stream (kernel_fn lines ~1829-1846), overlapping the pooler GEMM and pre_expert_norm. The rewrite replaces moe_align at T>32 with moe_route_list. If moe_route_list stays on the side stream as specified, the incumbent comparison is fair. If it lands on the main stream, part of any verify_16/32 delta is lost overlap rather than GEMM time. Read the profile's per-kernel times, not the headline.

marlin-block-m-cap-16: this is the incumbent Marlin configuration at T=128/256 (block_m clamped to 16), so it sets the bar the replaced sum must beat. A different cap would move the bar but not the new kernels' own time. Not a confounder for the rewrite's milestones, which are judged on the replaced kernels' own time.

post-expert-norm-triton-small-t: gated to small T. At T>32 both master and the rewrite end in SGLang's fused_post_expert_norm_weighted_sum (the patch keeps that call), so the numerical and launch path after w2 is the same. No confound, provided the new w2 output keeps Marlin's y layout and dtype ([M*8, 4096] bf16, slot order matching local_ids).
interference: No companions. This is a rewrite stage judged on the replaced kernels' per-kernel time in the verify_16/32 profiles against Marlin's 254-450 us and the floor. The gate (tokens > 32) leaves decode_* and verify_1 as built-in controls, and the incumbent kernels sit in master's own profile. An ab-revert of stack-align-par-sidestream-sliding1 would only re-measure the align overlap, not the GEMM rewrite. The open question is correctness and survival (does it fault?), and only the next stage answers that.
rules_flags: Fix (1) is not allowed. It spawns a torch.multiprocessing child, or a subprocess that imports the load_inline build dir, to contain the sticky fault. TASK.md Rules: 'A submission is rejected if it ... starts processes'. The workspace precedent is the same (muse_attention_decode full-decode-cuda-fp8-qk-mma left out cuobjdump because a subprocess is a rules violation). Remove it. Keep the in-process per-kernel torch.cuda.synchronize() and prints in prepare(), and the 1-CTA dequant8 + one mma tile micro self-test (it is prepare-time, untimed, on synthetic data). Accept that a fault kills the run, and run it as `okc check`; the failed predecessor 1bba1bab70da4f61 was mode submit.
torch.cuda.synchronize() and printing are fine in prepare() only. Confirm that no sync or print of per-kernel CUDA-event times reaches kernel_fn.

Setting TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST / extra_cuda_cflags for load_inline is build configuration, as on master, so it is allowed. load_inline's own nvcc/ninja invocation is the existing, accepted build mechanism. Do not add any other process launch.

Weights: 'retiled 32 experts losslessly' must stay NVFP4 bit-exact (codes plus fp8 scales, repacked only). The dequant to bf16 happens in-register inside the kernel, which is allowed. The __hmul2 scale fold must not pre-multiply and store weights in bf16.
open_questions: Without a child process, is there a rules-clean way to survive a sticky 715? I don't believe so in-process. Either accept losing a check per fault, or first run the 1-CTA micro self-test on its own as a tiny diagnostic check, with the full launch disabled, to clear dequant8 and the mma tile cheaply.

Are the ldmatrix/mma.sync calls reached by every lane of each warp at the chunk and item boundaries (nn_n < 8*NF_MAX, the bx >= total early return, the kk >= nk tail of load_meta)? A non-converged .sync.aligned collective also traps as an illegal instruction, and neither swap would fix that.
Does moe_route_list launch on state['side_stream'] where master's _expert_dispatch runs now, and does the w13 launch wait on it through the existing main_stream.wait_stream(side_stream)?
221184 B dynamic smem at 256 threads leaves one CTA per SM. Does the 132-CTA persistent grid still keep enough bytes in flight to beat ~1.2 TB/s at T=128, where many local experts get few routes?
